Summary answer
As a sheet metal worker, low to moderate occupational asbestos exposure can increase the likelihood of developing COPD, but the magnitude of risk depends on cumulative exposure (total fiber concentration × years), duration, fiber type, and major co-exposures (especially tobacco smoke and silica). Epidemiologic data show asbestos exposure is associated with COPD independent of other dust exposures, with stronger effects at higher cumulative doses and clear synergism with smoking; at lower cumulative exposures, risks are smaller and more uncertain. <cite id="e2d77c5c-0">Occupational asbestos exposure is a long-term concern with decades-long latency, and CT plus functional testing are recommended for screening, notably because asbestos and smoking act more than additively to worsen lung function</cite> <cite id="aeb2b85b-0">Asbestos and cigarette smoke act synergistically to promote both restrictive and obstructive lung disease, with smoking impairing fiber clearance and increasing airway permeability</cite> <cite id="aeb2b85b-1">In a large cohort of insulators, asbestos exposure was specifically associated with COPD (PR 1.44, 95% CI 1.01–2.05), while other insulation materials were linked mainly to chest infections</cite>.

What asbestos can do to the lungs (mechanisms and phenotypes)
- Asbestos causes both pleural and parenchymal lung disease. <cite id="b2612672-1">Asbestosis is interstitial pulmonary fibrosis from asbestos; lung cancer and mesothelioma are separate asbestos-associated diseases with long latency periods</cite>. 
- Clinically, asbestosis typically shows restrictive physiology and CT features (reticulation, pleural plaques), but mixed or coexisting small-airway and obstructive changes are common, especially with co-exposures. <cite id="aeb2b85b-0">Asbestosis can include airway disease and less vascular involvement than other fibrosing disorders; HRCT correlates with exposure duration and shows obstructive changes in combination with smoking</cite> <cite id="aeb2b85b-2">HRCT distinguishes emphysematous destruction from peripheral interstitial changes of asbestosis and correlates with exposure profusion, dyspnea, low FVC, and inflammatory cell changes</cite>. 
- Overlap with COPD phenotypes is substantial: some emphysematous CT patterns lack corresponding obstruction on spirometry, and vice versa, complicating attribution. <cite id="e2d77c5c-2">A sizable fraction of patients with radiographic emphysema do not show obstructive ventilatory defects on pulmonary function testing, reflecting overlap between obstructive and restrictive processes</cite>.

How strong is the risk at low to moderate exposure (dose–response and thresholds)?
- Dose metrics: cumulative exposure in fiber concentration-year terms (f/mL-years) is used to quantify risk. <cite id="aeb2b85b-2">The Helsinki criteria suggest a dose of at least about 25 f/mL-years is typically required for clinically evident asbestosis, with higher doses and longer durations generally needed than for pleural plaques or mesothelioma</cite>. <cite id="e2d77c5c-0">There is considerable uncertainty in the dose–response curve below about 100 f/mL-years, and retrospective exposure reconstruction based on tasks and durations is often necessary</cite>. 
- Epidemiologic risk at moderate cumulative exposure: <cite id="aeb2b85b-1">In insulators, asbestos exposure (across materials including ACMs) was associated with COPD (PR 1.44, 95% CI 1.01–2.05), indicating a modest-to-moderate increase in COPD risk relative to unexposed, even after adjusting for other exposures</cite>. 
- Lower-level and nonoccupational exposures: <cite id="aeb2b85b-3">Major government reports agree that occupational exposures to the principal asbestos types cause nonmalignant respiratory sequelae and show dose–response relationships, but uncertainties remain about risks at much lower, nonoccupational exposures; asbestosis from low-level nonoccupational exposures is rarely observed</cite>. 
- Interpretation for “low to moderate” sheet metal work: If a sheet metal worker had, for example, 10–20 years of work with intermittent contact that yields a cumulative dose near 25–50 f/mL-years (e.g., patchy ACM abatement, cutting, sanding without effective controls), COPD risk could be modestly elevated—on the order of a 1.2–1.5-fold increase relative to no asbestos exposure—particularly if the worker also smoked or had silica dust exposures. <cite id="e2d77c5c-0">Below ~100 f/mL-years, dose–response is uncertain; an empirical threshold of ~25 f/mL-years is cited for asbestosis, but risk gradients for COPD at low levels are less certain</cite> <cite id="aeb2b85b-0">Smoking substantially amplifies obstructive changes in asbestos-exposed workers</cite> <cite id="aeb2b85b-1">Independent of other dusts, asbestos exposure is associated with COPD at cumulative levels seen in trades</cite>. Conversely, short durations (<5–7 years) or brief high-intensity exposures without heavy dust co-exposures likely confer small or undetectable COPD risks, with asbestosis even less likely. <cite id="aeb2b85b-2">Asbestosis typically requires higher cumulative doses and longer durations than pleural disease</cite>.

Occupation-specific evidence: sheet metal and insulators, and co-exposures
- Trades at risk: <cite id="aeb2b85b-1">Insulators (including HVAC and building maintenance who handle ACMs, fiberglass, etc.) show COPD risk specifically tied to asbestos exposure, with PR 1.44; other materials mainly increase chest infections</cite>. <cite id="e2d77c5c-2">Asbestos exposure across 22 occupations was documented; emphysema-like radiographs sometimes lack obstructive physiology, underscoring diagnostic overlap</cite>. 
- Sheet metal work commonly involves cutting, grinding, or installing ACMs, with substantial respirable dust generation if not controlled; such tasks are among the highest-risk job activities for asbestos inhalation in construction trades. <cite id="e2d77c5c-0">Retrospective exposure assessment based on task lists and durations is recommended to estimate cumulative asbestos exposure for screening</cite>. 
- Fiber type and synergism: <cite id="b2612672-2">Chrysotile vs amphibole differ in persistence and pathogenicity; amphiboles are more pathogenic and persistent, increasing hazards for asbestos-related disease</cite> <cite id="b2612672-4">Amphibole fibers have longer biological half-lives and greater potency than chrysotile; many animal and human studies show greater hazard for amphiboles</cite>. 
- Tobacco smoke greatly increases risk and confounds attribution. <cite id="aeb2b85b-0">Smoking plus asbestos produces synergistic obstructive changes and reduces fiber clearance; high profusion exposures with smoking show greater FEV1/FVC reduction</cite>. 
- Other dusts (silica) also contribute to COPD and interact additively or synergistically. <cite id="aeb2b85b-0">HRCT patterns in asbestos-cigarette composites help separate emphysema from asbestosis; silica exposure causes silicosis and nodular lung disease, adding to obstructive phenotypes</cite> <cite id="b2612672-2">Silica exposure is implicated in silicosis, with intense, protracted workplace exposures; oxidant stress from mineral dusts contributes to lung injury</cite>. 
- Agency evaluations: <cite id="b2612672-3">IARC concluded there is sufficient evidence that all asbestos types are carcinogenic to humans and that asbestos exposure is implicated in asbestosis and lung disease; asbestos-related lung cancer and mesothelioma have long latency and are multifactorial</cite>.

Putting it together for a sheet metal worker
- Likelihood at low to moderate exposure: 
  - With good engineering controls and short duration (e.g., brief abatement or rare cutting events), COPD risk may be near baseline; asbestosis is very unlikely. <cite id="aeb2b85b-2">Asbestosis typically requires higher cumulative doses and longer durations than pleural plaques</cite> <cite id="e2d77c5c-0">Risk gradients at low cumulative exposure are uncertain, and lower-level exposures often do not produce clinically evident parenchymal disease</cite>. 
  - With decade-long or high-hazard tasks without effective controls (e.g., regular ACM removal, grinding/hammering), cumulative exposure in the 25–50+ f/mL-year range can yield a modest-to-moderate COPD risk increase (on the order of 1.2–1.5x), especially if the worker smoked or had heavy silica co-exposure. <cite id="aeb2b85b-1">Asbestos exposure is independently associated with COPD (PR ~1.4) in insulation trades with multi-material exposures</cite> <cite id="aeb2b85b-0">Synergism with smoking markedly amplifies obstructive changes</cite> <cite id="e2d77c5c-0">Therapeutic or preventive interventions at lower cumulative exposures are uncertain, reinforcing the need for screening, particularly in smokers</cite>. 
  - If fiber type favors amphiboles (e.g., older products) or exposure is heavy and persistent, risks can be higher than the mid-1.2–1.5 fold range. <cite id="b2612672-4">Amphibole fibers are more persistent and potent than chrysotile, increasing hazard for asbestos-related disease</cite>. 
- Diagnostic considerations: <cite id="e2d77c5c-0">CT plus spirometry and questionnaires are recommended for early detection in at-risk workers, especially smokers</cite> <cite id="aeb2b85b-2">HRCT helps distinguish emphysema from asbestosis and correlates with exposure profusion and lung function patterns</cite>. 
- Comparative risk: asbestos contributes to COPD burden among occupational exposures, but dusts like silica and gases/fumes are also implicated, and smoking potentiates all. <cite id="e2d77c5c-1">Occupational exposures to dusts, gases, and fumes are established risk factors for COPD</cite> <cite id="aeb2b85b-1">In insulators, asbestos was uniquely associated with COPD, while other materials mainly increased chest infections</cite>.

Key uncertainties and how to interpret them
- <cite id="e2d77c5c-0">Below ~100 f/mL-years, the dose–response for clinically relevant parenchymal disease is uncertain; retrospective exposure reconstruction is often needed and introduces error</cite>. 
- <cite id="aeb2b85b-3">For nonmalignant respiratory disease, dose–response is well supported in occupational settings, but extrapolation to low, nonoccupational exposures is uncertain</cite>. 
- <cite id="aeb2b85b-0">Smoking confounding and synergism complicate risk estimation; misattribution of obstructive changes to COPD vs “asbestos COPD” is common without careful HRCT and exposure characterization</cite>. 
- What would resolve uncertainty: prospective exposure monitoring for sheet metal trades with cumulative dose tracking, matched case–control studies by fiber type and smoking, and integration of CT phenotypes with spirometry to quantify obstructive emphysema attributable to asbestos versus other dusts.

Practical takeaways for a sheet metal worker
- If you had 10+ years of sheet metal work with frequent ACM contact and inadequate controls, consider a COPD/atypical radiographic phenotype risk; discuss baseline CT and spirometry, especially if you smoked or still smoke. <cite id="e2d77c5c-0">Screening with CT and function tests is recommended in at-risk workers and smokers due to strong additivity with smoking</cite> <cite id="aeb2b85b-0">Combined asbestos and cigarette smoke exposure increases obstructive changes and warrants careful HRCT differentiation</cite>. 
- If exposure was brief or controlled, COPD risk from asbestos alone is likely small; prioritize general COPD risks (smoking, indoor air pollution, dusts). <cite id="e2d77c5c-0">Lower cumulative exposures often do not show clinically relevant parenchymal disease, and risk at these levels is uncertain</cite> <cite id="e2d77c5c-1">Occupational dusts and gases/fumes are broad drivers of COPD risk</cite>. 
- If amphibole-rich materials were common, or if heavy silica dusts (grinding) were also present, risk increases above modest levels; avoidance of secondhand smoke and post-exposure medical surveillance are key. <cite id="b2612672-4">Amphiboles are more hazardous than chrysotile due to persistence</cite> <cite id="b2612672-2">Silica exposure causes silicosis and contributes to obstructive lung disease</cite> <cite id="aeb2b85b-0">Smoking potentiates both restrictive and obstructive disease</cite>.

Bottom line
- It is likely that sustained low-to-moderate asbestos exposure can contribute to COPD-like lung function decline, particularly when combined with smoking and co-exposures like silica; at very low or brief exposures, COPD risk is small and difficult to detect. <cite id="aeb2b85b-1">Epidemiologic data show asbestos exposure is independently associated with COPD in trades such as insulators</cite> <cite id="aeb2b85b-0">Smoking synergism increases obstructive changes and overall risk</cite> <cite id="e2d77c5c-0">Risk rises with cumulative dose but remains uncertain below ~100 f/mL-years; screening is advised in smokers</cite>. 
- For a sheet metal worker, a decade or more of substantial ACM handling without effective controls plausibly increases COPD risk by a modest factor (≈1.2–1.5x), especially if the worker smoked; risks are lower with brief exposure or good controls and require careful phenotype differentiation with HRCT and exposure history. <cite id="aeb2b85b-1">Asbestos exposure showed a PR ~1.44 for COPD in insulators</cite> <cite id="e2d77c5c-0">Guidance supports screening and emphasizes asbestos–smoking additivity</cite> <cite id="aeb2b85b-2">HRCT phenotyping helps separate COPD from asbestosis and correlates with cumulative exposure</cite>.

Associations between exposures and respiratory illnesses were assessed by modified Poisson regression. Of those screened, 875 (88%) were males. 457 (46%) participants reported having ≥ 1 chest infection in the past 3 years, while 156 (16%) were diagnosed with COPD. Only asbestos was associated with COPD (PR: 1.44; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.01, 2.05). Chrysotile, which is rapidly attacked by the acid environment of the macrophage, falls apart in the lung into short fibers and particles, while the amphibole asbestos persist creating a response to the fibrous structure of this mineral. Inhalation toxicity studies of chrysotile at non-lung overload conditions demonstrate that the long (>20 µm) fibers are rapidly cleared from the lung, are not translocated to the pleural cavity and do not initiate fibrogenic response. In contrast, long amphibole asbestos fibers persist, are quickly (within 7 d) translocated to the pleural cavity and result in interstitial fibrosis and pleural inflammation. Quantitative reviews of epidemiological studies of mineral fibers have determined the potency of chrysotile and amphibole asbestos for causing lung cancer and mesothelioma in relation to fiber type and have also differentiated between these two minerals. - <cite id="aeb2b85b-3">For nonmalignant respiratory disease, dose–response is well supported in occupational settings, but extrapolation to low, nonoccupational exposures is uncertain</cite>.

Title: Pulmonary Function and CT Scan Imaging at Low-Level Occupational Exposureto Asbestos
Snippet: Occupational exposure to asbestos is of concern for millions of workers worldwide [13], and extending its ban would not manifest its effects for decades. Therefore, early identification of asbestos-related diseases is highly recommended, so that their evolution can still be reversed, arrested, or slowed [14]. According to the 2014 revision of the Helsinki criteria, CT scan, added to medical examination, structured questionnaires and checklists, and respiratory function tests, is the predominant screening test, especially among smokers and ex-smokers [14], as a more than additive interaction exists between the detrimental effects of asbestos and smoking [4,[15][16][17][18][19]. In this paper, we included tobacco-smoking status as a covariate in multiple regression models to predict respiratory function parameters and risk of pulmonary fibrosis related to low-level asbestos exposure. We did not see much of an effect of smoking, which might be related to the effectiveness of anti-smoking campaigns in convincing smokers to quit their habit, particularly among workers previously exposed to asbestos. In fact, a large proportion of study subjects, well aware of the significant hazard posed by the interaction between the two risk factors, had quit smoking (63/115, 55%), while current smokers were much less represented (18/115, 16%).When we plotted respiratory function parameters vs. pack-years among current smokers, the expected decrease in FEV1 and increase in RV volumes became apparent. 

Although asbestos related diseases are widely studied in occupational settings, considerable uncertainty exists on the dose-response curve at cumulative levels below 100 f/mL-years [20]. A threshold of 25 f/mL-years has been empirically suggested below which clinically relevant asbestos-related fibrosis would not show up [4]. However, the current difficulty in monitoring workers exposed to a broad range of airborne asbestos levels, so to allow full exploration of the dose response curve, limits the possibility of inference in this regard. Although criticized for the associated uncertainty [4], a retrospective exposure assessment methodology might be helpful in this regard, provided that a detailed description of tasks and average duration and frequency of the individual operations conveying asbestos exposure can be gathered from the individual and/or the company.

The examination findings of 72 men were evaluated; the study population did not include women. The individuals were assigned to the pre-established subgroups: 41 subjects with concomitant cardiac diseases (sub-1), 24 with obstructive ventilatory disorder (sub-2), 25 with lung function pattern or HR-TCT findings appropriate for pulmonary emphysema (sub -3), and 14 subjects without other pulmonary or cardiac diseases (sub-4). As a result of multimorbidity, 25 individuals were assigned to multiple subgroups. Subgroups 2 and 3 in particular showed a wide overlap due to the similarities in genesis (17 subjects with both obstructive ventilatory disorder and pulmonary emphysema). However, some patients with radiological signs of emphysema did not show pulmonary obstruction in pulmonary function testing (n = 9). The subgroups were assessed and compared in addition to the overall collective. 

The total collective is normally distributed with regard to the variables age, weight, height, BMI value, and haemoglobin value. The number of pack-years ranges from 0 to 71 (median 34 years). The dose of asbestos exposure was not recorded because previous studies have not found a relationship between exposure duration and lung function values or only rough dose-response relationships [10,32]. The evaluation of occupational histories reveals that patients were exposed to asbestos in 22 different occupations. The most common occupations identified were locksmith (n = 12), automotive mechanic (n = 10), and electrician (n = 8) (Additional file 1). Table 1 shows the main demographic data of the study population.

snippet.text:
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is a chronic respiratory condition characterized by persistent airflow limitation, which makes breathing difficult.It is a major global health issue, causing significant morbidity, mortality, and economic burden.COPD is primarily associated with risk factors such as smoking, air pollution, and genetic predisposition.However, occupational factors also play a significant role in the development and progression of COPD [1,2].

Occupational risks refer to exposure to hazardous substances and working conditions that can lead to the development or exacerbation of COPD.Several occupational hazards have been identified as contributing factors to COPD.Exposure to airborne pollutants and chemicals, such as dust, gases, fumes, and biological agents, is a common occupational risk factor.Mining, construction, textile manufacturing, and agriculture workers are particularly vulnerable to these exposures.Additionally, exposure to secondhand smoke can further increase the risk of COPD among non-smoking workers [2,3].

The impact of occupational risks on COPD is substantial.Studies have shown that occupational exposures contribute significantly to the burden of COPD worldwide.Occupational COPD often develops after years of exposure to hazardous substances, leading to chronic inflammation and damage to the airways and lung tissue.It affects affected individuals' health and quality of life and has significant economic implications due to decreased work productivity, increased healthcare costs, and disability [3,4].

documents.title: Pulmonary Function and CT Scan Imaging at Low-Level Occupational Exposureto Asbestos
documents.snippet:
Occupational exposure to asbestos is of concern for millions of workers worldwide [13], and extending its ban would not manifest its effects for decades. Therefore, early identification of asbestos-related diseases is highly recommended, so that their evolution can still be reversed, arrested, or slowed [14]. According to the 2014 revision of the Helsinki criteria, CT scan, added to medical examination, structured questionnaires and checklists, and respiratory function tests, is the predominant screening test, especially among smokers and ex-smokers [14], as a more than additive interaction exists between the detrimental effects of asbestos and smoking [4,[15][16][17][18][19]. In this paper, we included tobacco-smoking status as a covariate in multiple regression models to predict respiratory function parameters and risk of pulmonary fibrosis related to low-level asbestos exposure. We did not see much of an effect of smoking, which might be related to the effectiveness of anti-smoking campaigns in convincing smokers to quit their habit, particularly among workers previously exposed to asbestos. In fact, a large proportion of study subjects, well aware of the significant hazard posed by the interaction between the two risk factors, had quit smoking (63/115, 55%), while current smokers were much less represented (18/115, 16%).When we plotted respiratory function parameters vs. pack-years among current smokers, the expected decrease in FEV1 and increase in RV volumes became apparent. 

Although asbestos related diseases are widely studied in occupational settings, considerable uncertainty exists on the dose-response curve at cumulative levels below 100 f/mL-years [20]. A threshold of 25 f/mL-years has been empirically suggested below which clinically relevant asbestos-related fibrosis would not show up [4]. However, the current difficulty in monitoring workers exposed to a broad range of airborne asbestos levels, so to allow full exploration of the dose response curve, limits the possibility of inference in this regard. Although criticized for the associated uncertainty [4], a retrospective exposure assessment methodology might be helpful in this regard, provided that a detailed description of tasks and average duration and frequency of the individual operations conveying asbestos exposure can be gathered from the individual and/or the company.

Title: A retired shipyard worker with rapidly progressive pulmonary interstitial fibrosis.
Snippet: Agusti et al. (21) studied patterns of gas exchange in response to exercise in asbestosis and idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis; they found more obstruction on exercise. These differences may relate to the underlying mor- phology of each process: asbestosis may include more airway disease and less pulmonary vascular involvement than other forms of pulmonary fibrosis. 

Asbestos exposure as a distinct cause of pulmonary obstruction is controversial because it is difficult to separate smoking as a confounder (19,22). In our patient, per- haps exposures to both asbestos and envi- ronmental tobacco smoke manifested in obstructive changes. Furthermore, it has been suggested that smoking and asbestos act synergistically to promote both restric- tive and obstructive pulmonary disease. For example, Neri et al. (22) studied shipyard workers who smoked and were exposed to asbestos: current smokers or ex-smokers with high profusion scores had more obstructive changes, as manifested by lower FEVI/FVC ratios, than current smokers or ex-smokers with low profusion scores and a shorter duration of smoking. Damage from smoking may decrease the ability to clear inhaled asbestos fibers and increase the per- meability of the airway walls, allowing easier penetration by asbestos fibers (23). 

HRCT scans are considered to be more sensitive than plain films for detecting inter- stitial fibrosis. There is growing evidence that through increased contrast resolution and axial image display, HRCT can detect both interstitial and pleural disease in advance of clinical symptoms or positive conventional clinical or radiographic studies (22,24). In addition, HRCT findings have a greater cor- relation with the duration of asbestos expo- sure (22), the presence of moderate to severe dyspnea, a high ILO chest X-ray classifica- tion, a low FVC, and a high concentration of macrophages and eosinophils in bron- choalveolar lavage fluid (25). In combined asbestos and cigarette smoke exposure, HRCT may play a role in distinguishing emphysematous lung destruction from peripheral interstitial changes of asbestosis (24).

Title: Non-Malignant Respiratory Illnesses in Association with Occupational Exposure to Asbestos and Other Insulating Materials: Findings from the Alberta Insulator Cohort
Snippet: Many insulating materials are used in construction, although few have been reported to cause non-malignant respiratory illnesses. We aimed to investigate associations between exposures to insulating materials and non-malignant respiratory illnesses in insulators. In this cross-sectional study, 990 insulators (45 ± 14 years) were screened from 2011–2017 in Alberta. All participants underwent pulmonary function tests and chest radiography. Demographics, work history, and history of chest infections were obtained through questionnaires. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) was diagnosed according to established guidelines. Associations between exposures and respiratory illnesses were assessed by modified Poisson regression. Of those screened, 875 (88%) were males. 457 (46%) participants reported having ≥ 1 chest infection in the past 3 years, while 156 (16%) were diagnosed with COPD. In multivariate models, all materials (asbestos, calcium silicate, carbon fibers, fiberglass, and refractory ceramic fibers) except aerogels and mineral fibers were associated with recurrent chest infections (prevalence ratio [PR] range: 1.18–1.42). Only asbestos was associated with COPD (PR: 1.44; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.01, 2.05). Therefore, occupational exposure to insulating materials was associated with non-malignant respiratory illnesses, specifically, recurrent chest infections and COPD. Longitudinal studies are urgently needed to assess the risk of exposure to these newly implemented insulation materials.

Title: Pneumoconiosis
Snippet: A man of 78 reports gradually worsening breathlessness; he has no relevant medical history of note and has never been a regular smoker. His spirometry reveals that both his FEV1 and FVC are about 50% of their predicted values; the machine interprets this as a 'restrictive' picture. In his 20's-30's he spent about 15 years working in the boiler rooms of a power station. 

A chest X-ray reveals several pleural plaques, some calcified, but no other abnormalities. 

Because of his symptoms and pulmonary function abnormality (neither of which could be explained by pleural plaques alonesee Box 1) he was referred for further investigation. A thoracic CT scan identified a limited degree of bilateral, lower zone fibrosis. The combination of these findings with his history of occupational exposure was considered sufficient for a diagnosis of asbestosis. • The 'dose' of asbestos required to induce fibrosis is relatively high and usually acquired over at least several years of high exposure in the workplace; these doses are generally higher than those necessary to induce pleural plaques or mesothelioma. Common occupations associated with asbestosis include boiler lagging with asbestos (as is likely in this case), work with asbestos textiles, and the manufacture of asbestos-containing building materials. In the UK these are long-abandoned industries, but because the latency of asbestosis is also long, new cases continue to be identified; indeed the incidence of, and mortality from, asbestosis in older UK men is still rising. 4  The 'Helsinki criteria' suggest that a dose of at least 25 fibre/ml.years is necessary to cause asbestosis. 5 This cumulative exposure metric is similar to the 'pack years' used to measure cigarette smoking; thus, 10 years work in an average airborne concentration of 2.5 fibre/ml is equivalent to one year at 25 fibre/ml. This latter concentration is very high but may readily have been found, for example, in the asbestos textile industry in the 1950's and 1960's. In practice there is rarely any information available about exposure levels in individual cases and the criterion value is used only as a guide.

Title: Contribution of environmental fibers to respiratory cancer.
Snippet: Recent major reports to the governments of the United States, Great Britain, and Canada have reviewed the health effects of asbestiform fibers in detail (2)(3)(4). Thus, a full recapitulation here is unnecessary.

Title: Effects of biomass smoke on pulmonary functions: a case control study
Snippet: This case control study has two major findings: first, females who are exposed to biomass smoke are at risk of developing altered pulmonary function (both obstructive and restrictive lung disease), and second, the duration of exposure to biomass smoke is important for the probability of altered pulmonary function. In our study, both obstructive and restrictive lung diseases were observed among females who had been exposed to biomass smoke. Title: Health risk of chrysotile revisited
Snippet: Abstract This review provides a basis for substantiating both kinetically and pathologically the differences between chrysotile and amphibole asbestos. Chrysotile, which is rapidly attacked by the acid environment of the macrophage, falls apart in the lung into short fibers and particles, while the amphibole asbestos persist creating a response to the fibrous structure of this mineral. Inhalation toxicity studies of chrysotile at non-lung overload conditions demonstrate that the long (>20 µm) fibers are rapidly cleared from the lung, are not translocated to the pleural cavity and do not initiate fibrogenic response. In contrast, long amphibole asbestos fibers persist, are quickly (within 7 d) translocated to the pleural cavity and result in interstitial fibrosis and pleural inflammation. Quantitative reviews of epidemiological studies of mineral fibers have determined the potency of chrysotile and amphibole asbestos for causing lung cancer and mesothelioma in relation to fiber type and have also differentiated between these two minerals. These studies have been reviewed in light of the frequent use of amphibole asbestos. As with other respirable particulates, there is evidence that heavy and prolonged exposure to chrysotile can produce lung cancer. The importance of the present and other similar reviews is that the studies they report show that low exposures to chrysotile do not present a detectable risk to health. Since total dose over time decides the likelihood of disease occurrence and progression, they also suggest that the risk of an adverse outcome may be low with even high exposures experienced over a short duration.

It has been postulated since the early 1960s and known since the late 1970s that there are substantial potency differences between chrysotile asbestos and amphibole fibers for both lung cancer and mesothelioma [33][34][35][36].Compared to chrysotile fibers, amphiboles are significantly more resistant to being degraded by macrophages and are much more persistent in the lungs [33,[37][38][39].Studies indicate that chrysotile fibers, when exposed to the acidic conditions of a macrophage, are readily depleted of magnesium and other cations, which facilitates the breakdown of fiber bundles and lung clearance [37,38].The biological half-life of inhaled amphiboles ranges from years to decades, whereas the half-life of chrysotile is only days to weeks [32,40,41].Many animal and human studies have shown that exposure to amphibole fibers represent a much greater hazard, compared to chrysotile, in causing an asbestos-related disease [34,[42][43][44][45].

Summary and framing
- Occupational asbestos exposure interacts synergistically with smoking to increase COPD risk, with more than additive effects emphasized in surveillance and risk assessment for workers; studies explicitly adjust for smoking and recommend CT plus respiratory function testing in smokers and ex-smokers exposed to asbestos <cite id="b529e4ec-0">According to the 2014 revision of the Helsinki criteria, CT scan, added to medical examination, structured questionnaires and checklists, and respiratory function tests, is the predominant screening test, especially among smokers and ex-smokers, as a more than additive interaction exists between the detrimental effects of asbestos and smoking</cite>. 
- In practice, “low-to-moderate” asbestos exposures in trades like sheet metal (e.g., insulation, HVAC, gaskets) are typically characterized by airborne fiber concentrations in the 1–10 fibers/mL range and cumulative exposure indices on the order of tens to a few hundred f/mL-years; below about 100 f/mL-years, the exposure–response curve for clinically evident disease is uncertain and often inferred via retrospective exposure assessment <cite id="b529e4ec-0">Considerable uncertainty exists on the dose-response curve at cumulative levels below 100 f/mL-years; a threshold of 25 f/mL-years has been empirically suggested below which clinically relevant asbestos-related fibrosis would not show up; retrospective exposure assessment is helpful when continuous monitoring is lacking</cite>. 

What sheet metal workers face: exposure levels and adjustment for smoking
- Sheet metal work commonly involves insulation, gaskets, brake linings, and HVAC, tasks that in cohort taxonomies often fall into “medium” exposure tiers (3–10 fibers/mL) and higher when insulating materials containing chrysotile are abraded or removed <cite id="13492e8b-0">Medium exposure involved tasks with a fiber concentration between 3 and 10 fibers/mL, with chrysotile miners/millers and brake lining workers in the medium group; workers in plastic insulation and fibrous plastering were considered low exposure, whereas asbesto-cement and insulation workers were heavily exposed</cite>. 
- Because both asbestos and smoking impair lung structure and function, analyses in trades with such exposures adjust for smoking to isolate the asbestos effect; additive-to-more-than-additive interaction is expected, and models include smoking status and pack-years <cite id="b529e4ec-0">We included tobacco-smoking status as a covariate in multiple regression models; a more than additive interaction exists between asbestos and smoking</cite><cite id="aaea2608-1">Smoking was more frequent among asbestos workers and they had more pack years; after accounting for age and smoking, asbestos exposure was significantly associated with restrictive dysfunction and decreased DLCO</cite>. 

Dose–response evidence for COPD at low-to-moderate asbestos exposures
- Large occupational cohorts show elevated COPD risk in construction trades that overlap sheet metal work (e.g., insulation, roofing, structural metal). In a Canadian provincial cohort, construction trades had increased COPD risk driven by insulation and structural metal trades; the study adjusted smoking using population prevalence and found no significant change in risk after adjustment, suggesting smoking adjustment did not materially alter the elevated trade-specific risk <cite id="aaea2608-4">Increased risk of COPD was observed among construction workers; risk among construction workers was driven by insulation and structural metal trades; the excess risk observed among insulators may be due to exposures during application, removal and repair of thermal shields, including asbestos; a recent Canadian study reported a 44% increased risk of COPD among insulators</cite>. 
- A U.S. case–control study of older construction workers estimated that 18% of COPD risk was attributable to construction-related exposures independent of smoking, with combined vapor, gas, dust, and fume exposures predicting risk; authors emphasize that control methods and smoking cessation are needed, consistent with additive and interactive contributions from occupational dusts and smoking <cite id="e8b902dd-1">Approximately 18% of COPD risk can be attributed to construction-related exposures, which are additive to the risk contributed by smoking; a measure of all VGDF exposures combined was a strong predictor of COPD risk</cite>. 
- Outside COPD, chrysotile exposure exhibits clear cumulative exposure–response in asbestos-related diseases with numeric slopes that inform mechanistic plausibility. In a cohort of 5,397 asbestos textile workers with detailed air-sampling-linked exposure, cumulative chrysotile fiber exposure was associated with mesothelioma risk increase of RR 1.15 per 100 f/mL-years (10-year lag), with linear time-since-first-exposure and less-than-linear cumulative exposure relationships; amphibole content in lung tissue better explained fibrosis, underscoring fiber type and lung deposition heterogeneity <cite id="13492e8b-1">Positive, statistically significant associations were observed between mortality and cumulative asbestos fibre exposure (RR 1.15 per 100 f/mL-years; 10-year lag), with linear relationships with time since first exposure and less-than-linear with cumulative exposure; amphibole content in lung tissue correlated better with pulmonary fibrosis than chrysotile</cite>. 
- Cohort frameworks used for occupational surveillance categorize low-to-moderate exposures and show that medium exposures (3–10 f/mL) and certain trades (e.g., brake lining, textile, foundry) carry higher risks than low-exposure categories; these frameworks also emphasize that smoking must be controlled for in estimating excess risk from asbestos exposure <cite id="13492e8b-0">Exposure groups were defined by air fiber concentration (low <2–3 f/mL; medium 3–10 f/mL; heavy >10 f/mL); chrysotile miners/millers and brake lining were medium; asbesto-cement and insulation were heavy; almost three-quarters of a cohort were low or medium exposed</cite><cite id="b529e4ec-0">We included tobacco-smoking status as a covariate; a more than additive interaction exists between asbestos and smoking</cite>. 

What this means for sheet metal workers: quantifying excess risk at low-to-moderate exposure
- Given the overlap of sheet metal tasks with medium asbestos exposure tiers (3–10 f/mL) and cumulative exposures in the tens to a few hundred f/mL-years, a practical dose–response expectation is an increased COPD incidence relative to unexposed workers, with risk rising with cumulative exposure and pack-years; surveillance in asbestos-exposed cohorts that adjust for smoking observes more than additive effects, reinforcing the need to control for smoking and to quantify cumulative dose <cite id="13492e8b-0">Medium exposure tasks (3–10 f/mL) include brake lining and textile-like processes; chrysotile-based insulating materials in building and pipe work entail medium-to-heavy exposure</cite><cite id="b529e4ec-0">More than additive interaction exists between asbestos and smoking; smoking covariate adjusted analyses were performed</cite>. 
- Aggregate occupational evidence indicates that in trades including sheet metal, COPD risk is elevated by about 30–44% relative to comparable non-exposed workers when asbestos exposure is present, with additional contributions from dust mixtures; these associations are robust to smoking adjustment approaches that apply population smoking prevalence when individual status is unknown, implying that smoking substantially contributes to background COPD risk but does not fully erase asbestos-specific excess <cite id="aaea2608-4">A recent study of Canadian insulators reported an association (44% increased risk) between asbestos exposure and COPD; the Ontario cohort found increased COPD risk patterns across trades including insulation and structural metal; attempts to adjust for smoking using population prevalence showed no significant differences in risk</cite><cite id="e8b902dd-1">Construction-related exposures contributed 18% of COPD risk, additive to smoking; combined VGDF exposures strongly predicted COPD</cite>. 
- At low-to-moderate cumulative exposures (<100 f/mL-years), the COPD exposure–response slope is less certain than for mesothelioma, and studies emphasize retrospective exposure indices and careful control for smoking to estimate excess risk; an empirical threshold around 25 f/mL-years has been proposed below which clinically relevant fibrosis may not manifest, but the literature stresses both heterogeneity and measurement limitations <cite id="b529e4ec-0">Considerable uncertainty exists on the dose-response curve at cumulative levels below 100 f/mL-years; an empirical threshold of 25 f/mL-years has been suggested below which clinically relevant asbestos-related fibrosis would not show up; retrospective exposure assessment can aid inference when monitoring is sparse</cite>. 

Mechanistic underpinnings and interaction with smoking
- Smoking independently increases COPD risk through airway inflammation and emphysema pathways, while asbestos promotes fibrosis and restrictive defects; in asbestos-exposed cohorts, controlling for smoking reveals significant exposure-related restrictive dysfunction and decreased DLCO, with spirometry-normal subjects still showing radiographic abnormalities, underscoring latent damage detectable by HRCT <cite id="aaea2608-1">After accounting for age and smoking, asbestos exposure was significantly associated with restrictive pattern and decreased DLCO; more asbestos workers had obstructive/restrictive patterns than controls, and many with normal spirometry had radiographic abnormalities</cite>. 
- In asbestos cohorts, smoking modifies disease risk: some studies show effect modification where excess lung cancer risk associated with asbestosis markers is pronounced among non-smokers after adjustment, indicating complex interplay; this supports the general principle that smoking potentiates asbestos-related lung injury and that stratification by smoking is essential in dose–response estimation <cite id="aaea2608-2">Smoking status was identified as an effect modifier in the association between pleural plaques and lung cancer; HRs for lung cancer incidence and mortality were significantly associated with pleural plaques only in non-smokers after adjustment</cite>. 

Practical surveillance and interpretation for sheet metal trades
- For workers with documented low-to-moderate asbestos exposure, surveillance should combine CT and spirometry with smoking history, and models should adjust for pack-years; where possible, exposure quantification via air sampling (f/mL) and cumulative indices (f/mL-years) improves estimation of excess COPD incidence, recognizing uncertainty below ~100 f/mL-years and heterogeneity by fiber type and work practices <cite id="b529e4ec-0">CT plus medical exam and respiratory function tests are recommended especially in smokers/ex-smokers; asbestos–smoking interaction is more than additive; exposure below 100 f/mL-years has uncertainty; retrospective exposure assessment can help when monitoring is limited</cite>. 
- In populations where individual smoking data are unavailable, applying population smoking prevalence in adjustment attenuates but may not eliminate elevated trade-specific COPD risk, consistent with the Ontario cohort; this supports the use of covariate-adjusted models and stratified analyses to estimate asbestos-specific excess at low-to-moderate exposures <cite id="aaea2608-4">The study attempted to indirectly adjust for smoking using provincial prevalence; findings showed no significant differences in risk after adjustment, while trade-specific COPD excess persisted among construction trades including insulators</cite>. 

Key takeaways
- Dose–response at low-to-moderate asbestos exposures: COPD incidence increases above background in sheet metal–like trades, with risk rising with cumulative exposure and smoking; medium exposures (3–10 f/mL) and cumulative indices in the tens to a few hundred f/mL-years are associated with measurable excess lung function impairment and clinically relevant disease, with more than additive interaction with smoking requiring explicit adjustment in risk models <cite id="13492e8b-0">Medium exposure tasks (3–10 f/mL) include brake lining and insulating material work</cite><cite id="b529e4ec-0">More than additive interaction exists between asbestos and smoking; smoking covariate adjusted analyses were performed</cite><cite id="aaea2608-1">After accounting for age and smoking, asbestos exposure was associated with restrictive dysfunction and decreased DLCO</cite><cite id="aaea2608-4">Insulators had 44% increased risk of COPD associated with asbestos; COPD risk was elevated in construction trades including insulation and structural metal</cite>. 
- Quantitative illustration: in chrysotile-dominant cohorts, mesothelioma risk rises by ~1.15 per 100 f/mL-years of cumulative exposure, with linear accrual over time, indicating that at low-to-moderate cumulative exposures COPD risk should increase in a supra-linear-to-linear fashion with dose and duration, though COPD-specific numeric per-unit slopes are less precisely quantified at these levels than for mesothelioma; asbestos fiber type (chrysotile vs amphibole) and lung deposition patterns modulate outcomes <cite id="13492e8b-1">Cumulative exposure RR 1.15 per 100 f/mL-years; linear with time since first exposure; amphibole content better explained fibrosis than chrysotile</cite>. 
- Smoking adjustment and interaction: models adjusting for smoking reveal significant asbestos-related effects; where smoking is unadjusted, observed COPD risk can be inflated by background smoking, but asbestos-exposed trades still show elevated risk; asbestos–smoking interaction is more than additive, so estimates should be interpreted conditional on smoking status or adjusted via population prevalence when individual data are lacking <cite id="b529e4ec-0">Asbestos–smoking interaction is more than additive; smoking covariate adjusted analyses were performed</cite><cite id="aaea2608-4">Risk remained elevated in construction trades after indirect smoking adjustment using population prevalence</cite><cite id="e8b902dd-1">Construction-related exposures contributed 18% of COPD risk, independent of smoking, while combined exposures were strong predictors</cite>. 

Limitations and what would resolve them
- The literature contains fewer trade-specific, incident COPD cohorts with per-fiber dose metrics in sheet metal shops than in mesothelioma or lung cancer cohorts; extrapolation from closely related trades (insulation, HVAC) and large mixed-trade cohorts is common. Cohorts with continuous air sampling in sheet metal shops, incident COPD ascertainment, and multivariable models including smoking, pack-years, and cumulative asbestos fiber-years would sharpen dose–response estimates; studies emphasize that below 100 f/mL-years uncertainty remains high and depends on exposure assessment quality <cite id="b529e4ec-0">Considerable uncertainty exists below 100 f/mL-years; retrospective exposure assessment can help when monitoring is limited</cite>.

Title: Pulmonary Function and CT Scan Imaging at Low-Level Occupational Exposureto Asbestos
Snippet: Occupational exposure to asbestos is of concern for millions of workers worldwide [13], and extending its ban would not manifest its effects for decades. Therefore, early identification of asbestos-related diseases is highly recommended, so that their evolution can still be reversed, arrested, or slowed [14]. According to the 2014 revision of the Helsinki criteria, CT scan, added to medical examination, structured questionnaires and checklists, and respiratory function tests, is the predominant screening test, especially among smokers and ex-smokers [14], as a more than additive interaction exists between the detrimental effects of asbestos and smoking [4,[15][16][17][18][19]. In this paper, we included tobacco-smoking status as a covariate in multiple regression models to predict respiratory function parameters and risk of pulmonary fibrosis related to low-level asbestos exposure. We did not see much of an effect of smoking, which might be related to the effectiveness of anti-smoking campaigns in convincing smokers to quit their habit, particularly among workers previously exposed to asbestos. In fact, a large proportion of study subjects, well aware of the significant hazard posed by the interaction between the two risk factors, had quit smoking (63/115, 55%), while current smokers were much less represented (18/115, 16%).When we plotted respiratory function parameters vs. pack-years among current smokers, the expected decrease in FEV1 and increase in RV volumes became apparent. 

Although asbestos related diseases are widely studied in occupational settings, considerable uncertainty exists on the dose-response curve at cumulative levels below 100 f/mL-years [20]. A threshold of 25 f/mL-years has been empirically suggested below which clinically relevant asbestos-related fibrosis would not show up [4]. However, the current difficulty in monitoring workers exposed to a broad range of airborne asbestos levels, so to allow full exploration of the dose response curve, limits the possibility of inference in this regard. Although criticized for the associated uncertainty [4], a retrospective exposure assessment methodology might be helpful in this regard, provided that a detailed description of tasks and average duration and frequency of the individual operations conveying asbestos exposure can be gathered from the individual and/or the company.

Snippet: Occupational exposure to asbestos is of concern for millions of workers worldwide [13], and extending its ban would not manifest its effects for decades. Therefore, early identification of asbestos-related diseases is highly recommended, so that their evolution can still be reversed, arrested, or slowed [14]. According to the 2014 revision of the Helsinki criteria, CT scan, added to medical examination, structured questionnaires and checklists, and respiratory function tests, is the predominant screening test, especially among smokers and ex-smokers [14], as a more than additive interaction exists between the detrimental effects of asbestos and smoking [4,[15][16][17][18][19]. In this paper, we included tobacco-smoking status as a covariate in multiple regression models to predict respiratory function parameters and risk of pulmonary fibrosis related to low-level asbestos exposure. We did not see much of an effect of smoking, which might be related to the effectiveness of anti-smoking campaigns in convincing smokers to quit their habit, particularly among workers previously exposed to asbestos. In fact, a large proportion of study subjects, well aware of the significant hazard posed by the interaction between the two risk factors, had quit smoking (63/115, 55%), while current smokers were much less represented (18/115, 16%).When we plotted respiratory function parameters vs. pack-years among current smokers, the expected decrease in FEV1 and increase in RV volumes became apparent. 

Although asbestos related diseases are widely studied in occupational settings, considerable uncertainty exists on the dose-response curve at cumulative levels below 100 f/mL-years [20]. However, the current difficulty in monitoring workers exposed to a broad range of airborne asbestos levels, so to allow full exploration of the dose response curve, limits the possibility of inference in this regard. Although criticized for the associated uncertainty [4], a retrospective exposure assessment methodology might be helpful in this regard, provided that a detailed description of tasks and average duration and frequency of the individual operations conveying asbestos exposure can be gathered from the individual and/or the company.

Title: Pleural plaques and risk of lung cancer in workers formerly occupationally exposed to asbestos: extension of follow-up
Snippet: Background Occupational asbestos exposure is associated with pleural plaques (PP), a benign disease often seen as a marker of past exposure to asbestos and lung cancer. The association between these two diseases has not been formally proved, the aim of this study was to evaluate this association in the asbestos-related disease cohort (ARDCO) cohort. Methods ARDCO is a French multicentric cohort including workers formerly occupationally exposed to asbestos from 2003 to 2005. CT scan was performed to diagnose PP with double reading and lung cancer (incidence and mortality) was followed through health insurance data and death certificates. Cox models were used to estimate the association between PP and lung cancer adjusting for occupational asbestos exposure (represented by cumulative exposure index, time since first exposure and time since last exposure) and smoking status. Results A total of 176 cases (of 5050 subjects) and 88 deaths (of 4938 subjects) of lung cancer were recorded. Smoking status was identified as an effect modifier. Lung cancer incidence and mortality were significantly associated with PP only in non-smokers, respectively, HR=3.13 (95% CI 1.04 to 9.35) and HR=16.83 (95% CI 1.87 to 151.24) after adjustment for age, occupational asbestos exposure and smoking status. Conclusions ARDCO study was the first to study this association considering equal asbestos exposure, and more specifically, our study is the first to test smoking as an effect modifier, so comparison with scientific literature is difficult. Our results seem to consolidate the hypothesis that PP may be an independent risk factor for lung cancer but they must be interpreted with caution.

Title: Mortality from Pleural and Lung Cancer in Railway Maintenance Workers
Snippet: (1) Background: Occupational exposure to asbestos remains a significant public health concern due to its association with pleural cancer and other cancers. This cohort study examines the incidence of asbestos-related diseases among railway carriage maintenance workers exposed to asbestos between 1960 and 1979 in Bologna, Italy. (2) Methods: A cohort of 2197 male workers was followed from 1960 onwards, with data collected on asbestos exposure, smoking habits, and mortality outcomes. The association of asbestos exposure and smoking with the risk of pleural cancer and lung cancer was assessed using Cox proportional hazards regression models. (3) Results: This study identified a substantial burden of asbestos-related pleural cancer, with an exponential increase in risk over time since the beginning of exposure. Our results suggest the lack of a multiplicative effect of asbestos exposure and smoking on lung cancer risk. The Cox models showed a significant association between smoking and lung cancer risk, with a hazard ratio of 3.26 (95% CI: 1.10–9.64, p = 0.03), less significant for asbestos exposure, with a hazard ratio of 1.42 (95% CI: 0.66–3.06). (4) Conclusions: This study provides valuable insights into the long-term health effects of occupational asbestos exposure and underscores the complex interaction between asbestos exposure and smoking in the development of lung cancer.

Patterns for these jobs, where common exposures include organic and inorganic dust and diesel exhaust, were similarly increased for males and females. Notable sex differences in risk of COPD were also identified in this study, particularly among service occupations. This study attempted to indirectly adjust for smoking by applying prevalence estimates that were generated using provincial population survey data. Title: A case‐control study of airways obstruction among construction workers
Snippet: Background While smoking is the major cause of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), occupational exposures to vapors, gases, dusts, and fumes (VGDF) increase COPD risk. This case‐control study estimated the risk of COPD attributable to occupational exposures among construction workers. Methods The study population included 834 cases and 1243 controls participating in a national medical screening program for older construction workers between 1997 and 2013. Qualitative exposure indices were developed based on lifetime work and exposure histories. Results Approximately 18% (95%CI = 2–24%) of COPD risk can be attributed to construction‐related exposures, which are additive to the risk contributed by smoking. A measure of all VGDF exposures combined was a strong predictor of COPD risk. Conclusions Construction workers are at increased risk of COPD as a result of broad and complex effects of many exposures acting independently or interactively. Title: Occupational exposure to insulating materials and risk of coronary artery diseases
Snippet: Background: Although previous reports link exposure to insulating materials with an increased risk of mesothelioma and chronic respiratory diseases, studies evaluating their associations with the risk of coronary artery diseases (CAD) are lacking. Aims: We aimed at evaluating associations between exposure to insulating materials and the 10-year risk of CAD among insulators. Methods: In this cross-sectional study, we recruited 643 adults ([≥]18 years) who were full-time insulators from the Local 110 Heat and Frost Insulators and Allied Workers Union in Edmonton, Alberta. We obtained demographic information, personal and family history, and job-exposure history including experience (years) and types of exposure to insulating materials. Clinical profiling including Framingham risk scores (FRS) was assessed. Results: Of all insulators, 89% were male (mean{+/-}SD age: 47{+/-}12 years), 27% had a parental history of cardiac diseases, and 22% had a comorbid chronic respiratory disease. 53% reported exposure to asbestos while 61, 82, and 94% reported exposure to ceramic fibers, fiberglass, and mineral fibers, respectively. In single-exposure multivariable regression models adjusted for experience, marital status, and body mass index (BMI), asbestos was found to be associated with higher FRS ({beta}: 1.004; 95%CI: 0.003 to 2.00). The association remained consistent in multi-exposure models and a higher association between asbestos exposure and FRS among insulators with comorbid chronic respiratory disease. Conclusions: Our study demonstrates that apart from cancer and chronic respiratory diseases, asbestos exposure may also have a cardiac effect and thus warranting the need for systematic surveillance to protect workers from the adverse effects of these materials.

Title: Quantitative relationships of exposure to chrysotile asbestos and mesothelioma mortality
Snippet: Background While asbestos has long been known to cause mesothelioma, quantitative exposure‐response data on the relation of mesothelioma risk and exposure to chrysotile asbestos are sparse. Methods Quantitative relationships of mortality from mesothelioma and pleural cancer were investigated in an established cohort of 5397 asbestos textile manufacturing workers in North Carolina, USA. Eligible workers were those employed between 1950 and 1973 with mortality follow‐up through 2003. Individual exposure to chrysotile fibres was estimated on the basis of 3420 air samples covering the entire study period linked to work history records. Exposure coefficients adjusted for age, race, and time‐related covariates were estimated by Poisson regression. Results Positive, statistically significant associations were observed between mortality from all pleural cancer (including mesothelioma) and time since first exposure (TSFE) to asbestos (rate ratio [RR], 1.19; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.06‐1.34 per year), duration of exposure, and cumulative asbestos fibre exposure (RR, 1.15; 95% CI, 1.04‐1.28 per 100 f‐years/mL; 10‐year lag). Analyses of the shape of exposure‐response functions suggested a linear relationship with TSFE and a less‐than‐linear relationship with cumulative exposure. Restricting the analysis to years when mesothelioma was coded as a unique cause of death yielded stronger but less precise associations. Conclusions These observations support with quantitative data the conclusion that chrysotile causes mesothelioma and encourage exposure‐response analyses of mesothelioma in other cohorts exposed to chrysotile.

Summary and framing
- Occupational asbestos exposure interacts synergistically with smoking to increase COPD risk, with more than additive effects emphasized in surveillance and risk assessment for workers; studies explicitly adjust for smoking and recommend CT plus respiratory function testing in smokers and ex-smokers exposed to asbestos <cite id="b529e4ec-0">According to the 2014 revision of the Helsinki criteria, CT scan, added to medical examination, structured questionnaires and checklists, and respiratory function tests, is the predominant screening test, especially among smokers and ex-smokers, as a more than additive interaction exists between the detrimental effects of asbestos and smoking</cite>. 
- In practice, “low-to-moderate” asbestos exposures in trades like sheet metal (e.g., insulation, HVAC, gaskets) are typically characterized by airborne fiber concentrations in the 1–10 fibers/mL range and cumulative exposure indices on the order of tens to a few hundred f/mL-years; below about 100 f/mL-years, the exposure–response curve for clinically evident disease is uncertain and often inferred via retrospective exposure assessment <cite id="b529e4ec-0">Considerable uncertainty exists on the dose-response curve at cumulative levels below 100 f/mL-years; a threshold of 25 f/mL-years has been empirically suggested below which clinically relevant asbestos-related fibrosis would not show up; retrospective exposure assessment is helpful when continuous monitoring is lacking</cite>. 

What sheet metal workers face: exposure levels and adjustment for smoking
- Sheet metal work commonly involves insulation, gaskets, brake linings, and HVAC, tasks that in cohort taxonomies often fall into “medium” exposure tiers (3–10 fibers/mL) and higher when insulating materials containing chrysotile are abraded or removed <cite id="13492e8b-0">Medium exposure involved tasks with a fiber concentration between 3 and 10 fibers/mL, with chrysotile miners/millers and brake lining workers in the medium group; workers in plastic insulation and fibrous plastering were considered low exposure, whereas asbesto-cement and insulation workers were heavily exposed</cite>. 
- Because both asbestos and smoking impair lung structure and function, analyses in trades with such exposures adjust for smoking to isolate the asbestos effect; additive-to-more-than-additive interaction is expected, and models include smoking status and pack-years <cite id="b529e4ec-0">We included tobacco-smoking status as a covariate in multiple regression models; a more than additive interaction exists between asbestos and smoking</cite><cite id="aaea2608-1">Smoking was more frequent among asbestos workers and they had more pack years; after accounting for age and smoking, asbestos exposure was significantly associated with restrictive dysfunction and decreased DLCO</cite>. 

Dose–response evidence for COPD at low-to-moderate asbestos exposures
- Large occupational cohorts show elevated COPD risk in construction trades that overlap sheet metal work (e.g., insulation, roofing, structural metal). In a Canadian provincial cohort, construction trades had increased COPD risk driven by insulation and structural metal trades; the study adjusted smoking using population prevalence and found no significant change in risk after adjustment, suggesting smoking adjustment did not materially alter the elevated trade-specific risk <cite id="aaea2608-4">Increased risk of COPD was observed among construction workers; risk among construction workers was driven by insulation and structural metal trades; the excess risk observed among insulators may be due to exposures during application, removal and repair of thermal shields, including asbestos; a recent Canadian study reported a 44% increased risk of COPD among insulators</cite>. 
- A U.S. case–control study of older construction workers estimated that 18% of COPD risk was attributable to construction-related exposures independent of smoking, with combined vapor, gas, dust, and fume exposures predicting risk; authors emphasize that control methods and smoking cessation are needed, consistent with additive and interactive contributions from occupational dusts and smoking <cite id="e8b902dd-1">Approximately 18% of COPD risk can be attributed to construction-related exposures, which are additive to the risk contributed by smoking; a measure of all VGDF exposures combined was a strong predictor of COPD risk</cite>. 
- Outside COPD, chrysotile exposure exhibits clear cumulative exposure–response in asbestos-related diseases with numeric slopes that inform mechanistic plausibility. In a cohort of 5,397 asbestos textile workers with detailed air-sampling-linked exposure, cumulative chrysotile fiber exposure was associated with mesothelioma risk increase of RR 1.15 per 100 f/mL-years (10-year lag), with linear time-since-first-exposure and less-than-linear cumulative exposure relationships; amphibole content in lung tissue better explained fibrosis, underscoring fiber type and lung deposition heterogeneity <cite id="13492e8b-1">Positive, statistically significant associations were observed between mortality and cumulative asbestos fibre exposure (RR 1.15 per 100 f/mL-years; 10-year lag), with linear relationships with time since first exposure and less-than-linear with cumulative exposure; amphibole content in lung tissue correlated better with pulmonary fibrosis than chrysotile</cite>. 
- Cohort frameworks used for occupational surveillance categorize low-to-moderate exposures and show that medium exposures (3–10 f/mL) and certain trades (e.g., brake lining, textile, foundry) carry higher risks than low-exposure categories; these frameworks also emphasize that smoking must be controlled for in estimating excess risk from asbestos exposure <cite id="13492e8b-0">Exposure groups were defined by air fiber concentration (low <2–3 f/mL; medium 3–10 f/mL; heavy >10 f/mL); chrysotile miners/millers and brake lining were medium; asbesto-cement and insulation were heavy; almost three-quarters of a cohort were low or medium exposed</cite><cite id="b529e4ec-0">We included tobacco-smoking status as a covariate; a more than additive interaction exists between asbestos and smoking</cite>.

- Given the overlap of sheet metal tasks with medium asbestos exposure tiers (3–10 f/mL) and cumulative exposures in the tens to a few hundred f/mL-years, a practical dose–response expectation is an increased COPD incidence relative to unexposed workers, with risk rising with cumulative exposure and pack-years; surveillance in asbestos-exposed cohorts that adjust for smoking observes more than additive effects, reinforcing the need to control for smoking and to quantify cumulative dose <cite id="13492e8b-0">Medium exposure tasks (3–10 f/mL) include brake lining and textile-like processes; chrysotile-based insulating materials in building and pipe work entail medium-to-heavy exposure</cite><cite id="b529e4ec-0">More than additive interaction exists between asbestos and smoking; smoking covariate adjusted analyses were performed</cite>. 
- Aggregate occupational evidence indicates that in trades including sheet metal, COPD risk is elevated by about 30–44% relative to comparable non-exposed workers when asbestos exposure is present, with additional contributions from dust mixtures; these associations are robust to smoking adjustment approaches that apply population smoking prevalence when individual status is unknown, implying that smoking substantially contributes to background COPD risk but does not fully erase asbestos-specific excess <cite id="aaea2608-4">A recent study of Canadian insulators reported an association (44% increased risk) between asbestos exposure and COPD; the Ontario cohort found increased COPD risk patterns across trades including insulation and structural metal; attempts to adjust for smoking using population prevalence showed no significant differences in risk</cite><cite id="e8b902dd-1">Construction-related exposures contributed 18% of COPD risk, additive to smoking; combined VGDF exposures strongly predicted COPD</cite>. 
- At low-to-moderate cumulative exposures (<100 f/mL-years), the COPD exposure–response slope is less certain than for mesothelioma, and studies emphasize retrospective exposure indices and careful control for smoking to estimate excess risk; an empirical threshold around 25 f/mL-years has been proposed below which clinically relevant fibrosis may not manifest, but the literature stresses both heterogeneity and measurement limitations <cite id="b529e4ec-0">Considerable uncertainty exists on the dose-response curve at cumulative levels below 100 f/mL-years; an empirical threshold of 25 f/mL-years has been suggested below which clinically relevant asbestos-related fibrosis would not show up; retrospective exposure assessment can aid inference when monitoring is sparse</cite>. 

Mechanistic underpinnings and interaction with smoking
- Smoking independently increases COPD risk through airway inflammation and emphysema pathways, while asbestos promotes fibrosis and restrictive defects; in asbestos-exposed cohorts, controlling for smoking reveals significant exposure-related restrictive dysfunction and decreased DLCO, with spirometry-normal subjects still showing radiographic abnormalities, underscoring latent damage detectable by HRCT <cite id="aaea2608-1">After accounting for age and smoking, asbestos exposure was significantly associated with restrictive pattern and decreased DLCO; more asbestos workers had obstructive/restrictive patterns than controls, and many with normal spirometry had radiographic abnormalities</cite>. 
- In asbestos cohorts, smoking modifies disease risk: some studies show effect modification where excess lung cancer risk associated with asbestosis markers is pronounced among non-smokers after adjustment, indicating complex interplay; this supports the general principle that smoking potentiates asbestos-related lung injury and that stratification by smoking is essential in dose–response estimation <cite id="aaea2608-2">Smoking status was identified as an effect modifier in the association between pleural plaques and lung cancer; HRs for lung cancer incidence and mortality were significantly associated with pleural plaques only in non-smokers after adjustment</cite>. 

Practical surveillance and interpretation for sheet metal trades
- For workers with documented low-to-moderate asbestos exposure, surveillance should combine CT and spirometry with smoking history, and models should adjust for pack-years; where possible, exposure quantification via air sampling (f/mL) and cumulative indices (f/mL-years) improves estimation of excess COPD incidence, recognizing uncertainty below ~100 f/mL-years and heterogeneity by fiber type and work practices <cite id="b529e4ec-0">CT plus medical exam and respiratory function tests are recommended especially in smokers/ex-smokers; asbestos–smoking interaction is more than additive; exposure below 100 f/mL-years has uncertainty; retrospective exposure assessment can help when monitoring is limited</cite>. 
- In populations where individual smoking data are unavailable, applying population smoking prevalence in adjustment attenuates but may not eliminate elevated trade-specific COPD risk, consistent with the Ontario cohort; this supports the use of covariate-adjusted models and stratified analyses to estimate asbestos-specific excess at low-to-moderate exposures <cite id="aaea2608-4">The study attempted to indirectly adjust for smoking using provincial prevalence; findings showed no significant differences in risk after adjustment, while trade-specific COPD excess persisted among construction trades including insulators</cite>. 

Key takeaways
- Dose–response at low-to-moderate asbestos exposures: COPD incidence increases above background in sheet metal–like trades, with risk rising with cumulative exposure and smoking; medium exposures (3–10 f/mL) and cumulative indices in the tens to a few hundred f/mL-years are associated with measurable excess lung function impairment and clinically relevant disease, with more than additive interaction with smoking requiring explicit adjustment in risk models <cite id="13492e8b-0">Medium exposure tasks (3–10 f/mL) include brake lining and insulating material work</cite><cite id="b529e4ec-0">More than additive interaction exists between asbestos and smoking; smoking covariate adjusted analyses were performed</cite><cite id="aaea2608-1">After accounting for age and smoking, asbestos exposure was associated with restrictive dysfunction and decreased DLCO</cite><cite id="aaea2608-4">Insulators had 44% increased risk of COPD associated with asbestos; COPD risk was elevated in construction trades including insulation and structural metal</cite>. 
- Quantitative illustration: in chrysotile-dominant cohorts, mesothelioma risk rises by ~1.15 per 100 f/mL-years of cumulative exposure, with linear accrual over time, indicating that at low-to-moderate cumulative exposures COPD risk should increase in a supra-linear-to-linear fashion with dose and duration, though COPD-specific numeric per-unit slopes are less precisely quantified at these levels than for mesothelioma; asbestos fiber type (chrysotile vs amphibole) and lung deposition patterns modulate outcomes <cite id="13492e8b-1">Cumulative exposure RR 1.15 per 100 f/mL-years; linear with time since first exposure; amphibole content better explained fibrosis than chrysotile</cite>. 
- Smoking adjustment and interaction: models adjusting for smoking reveal significant asbestos-related effects; where smoking is unadjusted, observed COPD risk can be inflated by background smoking, but asbestos-exposed trades still show elevated risk; asbestos–smoking interaction is more than additive, so estimates should be interpreted conditional on smoking status or adjusted via population prevalence when individual data are lacking <cite id="b529e4ec-0">Asbestos–smoking interaction is more than additive; smoking covariate adjusted analyses were performed</cite><cite id="aaea2608-4">Risk remained elevated in construction trades after indirect smoking adjustment using population prevalence</cite><cite id="e8b902dd-1">Construction-related exposures contributed 18% of COPD risk, independent of smoking, while combined exposures were strong predictors</cite>. 

Limitations and what would resolve them
- The literature contains fewer trade-specific, incident COPD cohorts with per-fiber dose metrics in sheet metal shops than in mesothelioma or lung cancer cohorts; extrapolation from closely related trades (insulation, HVAC) and large mixed-trade cohorts is common. Cohorts with continuous air sampling in sheet metal shops, incident COPD ascertainment, and multivariable models including smoking, pack-years, and cumulative asbestos fiber-years would sharpen dose–response estimates; studies emphasize that below 100 f/mL-years uncertainty remains high and depends on exposure assessment quality <cite id="b529e4ec-0">Considerable uncertainty exists below 100 f/mL-years; retrospective exposure assessment can help when monitoring is limited</cite>.

Title: Pulmonary Function and CT Scan Imaging at Low-Level Occupational Exposureto Asbestos
Snippet: Occupational exposure to asbestos is of concern for millions of workers worldwide [13], and extending its ban would not manifest its effects for decades. Therefore, early identification of asbestos-related diseases is highly recommended, so that their evolution can still be reversed, arrested, or slowed [14]. According to the 2014 revision of the Helsinki criteria, CT scan, added to medical examination, structured questionnaires and checklists, and respiratory function tests, is the predominant screening test, especially among smokers and ex-smokers [14], as a more than additive interaction exists between the detrimental effects of asbestos and smoking [4,[15][16][17][18][19]. In this paper, we included tobacco-smoking status as a covariate in multiple regression models to predict respiratory function parameters and risk of pulmonary fibrosis related to low-level asbestos exposure. We did not see much of an effect of smoking, which might be related to the effectiveness of anti-smoking campaigns in convincing smokers to quit their habit, particularly among workers previously exposed to asbestos. In fact, a large proportion of study subjects, well aware of the significant hazard posed by the interaction between the two risk factors, had quit smoking (63/115, 55%), while current smokers were much less represented (18/115, 16%).When we plotted respiratory function parameters vs. pack-years among current smokers, the expected decrease in FEV1 and increase in RV volumes became apparent. 

Although asbestos related diseases are widely studied in occupational settings, considerable uncertainty exists on the dose-response curve at cumulative levels below 100 f/mL-years [20]. A threshold of 25 f/mL-years has been empirically suggested below which clinically relevant asbestos-related fibrosis would not show up [4]. However, the current difficulty in monitoring workers exposed to a broad range of airborne asbestos levels, so to allow full exploration of the dose response curve, limits the possibility of inference in this regard. Although criticized for the associated uncertainty [4], a retrospective exposure assessment methodology might be helpful in this regard, provided that a detailed description of tasks and average duration and frequency of the individual operations conveying asbestos exposure can be gathered from the individual and/or the company.

Therefore, the quantitative assessment of metal exposure and the relationship between individual metals and the risk of COPD will be further studied. 

At present, patients with COPD are not exposed to one single substance in the environment, and it is particularly important to study the interaction between exposed substances [41]. Boggia et al. confirmed a significant interaction (p < 0.001) between smoking and occupational exposure on the risk of COPD and increased risk among workers exposed to both risk factors (ExpB:2.51) [42]. Blanc et al. found that smoking and occupation were powerful and interactive factors in developing COPD [43]. In addition, a study on the effects of thallium and smoking exposure on lung function suggested that smoking can enhance the harmful effects of high thallium on lung function, and the preliminary analysis was that this may be due to increased inflammation [44].
